name: Fault-tolerant Network
description: There is a classroom with two rows of computers. There are $$$n$$$ computers in each row and each computer has its own grade. Computers in the first row have grades $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ and in the second row — $$$b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$$$. Initially, all pairs of neighboring computers in each row are connected by wire (pairs $$$(i, i + 1)$$$ for all $$$1 \le i \lt n$$$), so two rows form two independent computer networks. Your task is to combine them into one common network by connecting one or more pairs of computers from different rows. Connecting the $$$i$$$-th computer from the first row and the $$$j$$$-th computer from the second row costs $$$|a_i - b_j|$$$. You can connect one computer to several other computers, but you need to provide at least a basic fault tolerance: you need to connect computers in such a way that the network stays connected, despite one of its computers failing. In other words, if one computer is broken (no matter which one), the network won't split into two or more parts. What is the minimum total cost to make a fault-tolerant network?
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. Next, $$$t$$$ cases follow. The first line of each test case contains the single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of computers in each row. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the grades of computers in the first row. The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$$$ ($$$1 \le b_i \le 10^9$$$) — the grades of computers in the second row. It's guaranteed that the total sum of $$$n$$$ doesn't exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer — the minimum total cost to make a fault-tolerant network.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1651C — Fault-tolerant Network [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
